newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week-Set to climb, seen undervalued.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week-Set to climb, seen undervalued.

text.p: UK gilts are undervalued and poised to climb this week, analysts said, with the improving trend in the PSBR likely to offer support when May's data are released on Tuesday.

"We're reasonably optimistic about gilts this week. We think the market is cheap and it should receive fairly good support at spreads of 150 basis points over Bunds," said HSBC Markets analyst Philip Tyson.

A Reuters poll forecasts May's PSBR at 3.0 billion stg. The figures should confirm government borrowing on a downward trend and some analysts said they were considering revising their 1997/98 estimates downwards.
"Some people have been revising their 1997/1998 forecasts recently which may help gilts," said Stephen Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
April's PSBR showed a surprise 36 million sterling surplus after the government's coffers were swelled by taxes and corporation tax receipts.

Full details of this month's auction will be announced on Tuesday at 1430 GMT, but analysts and traders said they were confident the market could easily absorb the supply of 7.25 percent 10-year gilts when it comes next week.
Other domestic indicators due this week will give gilts an insight into consumer activity in May.
On Wednesday, May retail sales data are due with sales forecast to rise by 0.1 percent on the month for year-on-year growth of 4.4 percent.
"Retail sales volumes have risen steadily in recent months, with quarter-on-quarter gains remaining around 1.0 percent," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.

Gilts will be less sensitive to May's M4 money supply data on Thursday which is expected to show a 0.7 percent rise on the month allowing the year-on-year growth rate to fall to 10.1 percent from 10.2 percent.
The rest of Europe is hooked on developments at the EU Amsterdam summit, which started on Monday.
But the forthcoming budget is overshadowing EMU news in the UK, with the focus firmly on the extent of fiscal tightening expected from Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown.

"Gilts should grind higher in the run-up to the (July 2) budget," Tyson said. "And any bad news from Amsterdam should be fairly limited. It looks as though the eventual outcome is moving towards monetary union anyway."

But a report by the National Audit Office into former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's budget projections, which Brown commissioned, was unlikely to find black holes in public finances that would justify any tax increases, Kleinwort Benson's Scott said.
"Our view is that there are no black holes in Clarke's budget projections."
The U.S. will extend its influence over gilts on Tuesday when industrial production data for May are released.
Stronger-than-expected data will reawaken speculation that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at the FOMC meeting on July 2.
